trivia_fact: Platform engineering emerged around 2020-2022 as a response to "you build it, you run it" burnout. The argument: instead of every team reinventing CI/CD, observability, and deployment, a dedicated platform team builds self-service tools. Gartner predicted it would be used by 80% of large organizations by 2026.

Netflix coined the "paved road" concept: instead of mandating tools, the platform team provides a well-lit, well-maintained path that is so easy to use that teams choose it voluntarily. Going off the paved road is allowed but means you maintain your own infrastructure.

Internal Developer Platforms (IDPs) are the central product of platform engineering. An IDP abstracts away infrastructure complexity so developers can deploy, monitor, and manage applications through a self-service interface without filing tickets or waiting for ops teams.

Backstage was created at Spotify in 2016 as their internal developer portal and open-sourced in 2020. It became a CNCF incubating project and is now the most widely adopted developer portal framework. Backstage provides a software catalog, scaffolding (templates), and a plugin ecosystem.

Golden paths (or "golden paths of development") describe the recommended, pre-configured way to accomplish common tasks on an IDP. Unlike rigid mandates, golden paths are opinionated defaults that teams can follow for the fastest, safest route from code to production.

The 2019 book "Team Topologies" by Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais provided the theoretical foundation for platform engineering. Its concept of "platform teams" providing self-service capabilities to "stream-aligned teams" gave organizations a vocabulary and structure for building internal platforms.

The core argument for platform engineering borrows from psychology: developers have limited cognitive load. Expecting every team to master Kubernetes, CI/CD, observability, security, and networking leads to shallow expertise everywhere. Platforms absorb infrastructure complexity so developers can focus on business logic.

A key tenet of platform engineering is treating the internal platform "as a product" with real users (developers), feedback loops, product managers, and roadmaps. This is a deliberate contrast to traditional IT operations, which treated infrastructure as a cost center delivering tickets rather than a product delivering value.
